parameters.quote: Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days of becoming aware of it, including incidents involving injury, property damage, or a safety-related shutdown. Incidents presenting an imminent risk of serious injury or fire shall be reported within 24 hours. A lack of confirmed root cause does not delay initial reporting.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days of becoming aware of it, including incidents involving injury, property damage, or a safety-related shutdown. Incidents presenting an imminent risk of serious injury or fire shall be reported within 24 hours. A lack of confirmed root cause does not delay initial reporting.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days of becoming aware of it, including incidents involving injury, property damage, or a safety-related shutdown. Incidents presenting an imminent risk of serious injury or fire shall be reported within 24 hours. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers within 5 calendar days when an incident indicates a potential safety hazard for their model; imminent hazards require notice within 24 hours. Reports shall include known incident circumstances and be updated as the investigation proceeds. A lack of confirmed root cause does not delay initial reporting.

parameters.quote: A failure rate above 5% shall trigger a corrective-action plan and regulator review, not an automatic sales prohibition; the regulator may impose proportionate restrictions where evidence shows they are necessary to protect safety. Full per-model results, including sample size, protocol, and failure rate, shall be provided to the relevant regulator and, before sale, to prospective customers considering that model.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% shall trigger a corrective-action plan and regulator review, not an automatic sales prohibition; the regulator may impose proportionate restrictions where evidence shows they are necessary to protect safety. Full per-model results, including sample size, protocol, and failure rate, shall be provided to the relevant regulator and, before sale, to prospective customers considering that model.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C using a regulator-approved protocol and a representative sample, with results reported as the percentage of tested units that fail. Manufacturers shall test before market launch and at least annually thereafter, and retest after a material design or manufacturing change. Full per-model results, including sample size, protocol, and failure rate, shall be provided to the relevant regulator and, before sale, to prospective customers considering that model. Results for other models need not be provided, and manufacturers are not required to publish per-model results to the general public. A failure rate above 5% shall trigger a corrective-action plan and regulator review, not an automatic sales prohibition; the regulator may impose proportionate restrictions where evidence shows they are necessary to protect safety.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems shall include a remote emergency shut-off capability at installation. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption of this standard, prioritizing units subject to a safety notice or elevated incident risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery systems shall include a remote emergency shut-off capability at installation. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption of this standard, prioritizing units subject to a safety notice or elevated incident risk.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery systems shall include a remote emergency shut-off capability at installation. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 6 years of adoption of this standard, prioritizing units subject to a safety notice or elevated incident risk. The shut-off must be accessible to authorized emergency responders and the manufacturer, operate safely during an emergency, and not prevent a household from locally disconnecting the system.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems shall include built-in fire suppression designed for the hazards of the system. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery systems shall include built-in fire suppression designed for the hazards of the system. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery systems shall include built-in fire suppression designed for the hazards of the system. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall document the suppression design and validate its performance through testing; the requirement does not replace applicable fire-safety testing or incident reporting.

parameters.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, investigate the causes, and submit incident data and a corrective-action plan to the regulator. The regulator shall determine whether a recall or other restrictions are warranted based on the evidence and risk, and may require them.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, investigate the causes, and submit incident data and a corrective-action plan to the regulator. The regulator shall determine whether a recall or other restrictions are warranted based on the evidence and risk, and may require them.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall provide customers with timely safety notices describing material risks, recommended precautions, and corrective actions. Notices shall be sent within 5 calendar days of identifying a potential safety hazard, or within 24 hours for an imminent hazard. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, investigate the causes, and submit incident data and a corrective-action plan to the regulator. The regulator shall determine whether a recall or other restrictions are warranted based on the evidence and risk, and may require them. The threshold applies to each model individually, not to a manufacturer’s company-wide incident rate.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Northwind’s requested figures: 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide last year; highest disclosed model rate is Hearth 10 at 6.4/100,000. Three thermal incidents were not reported to regulators. Hearth 10’s 55°C sustained-heat failure rate is 6.2%. Remote shut-off coverage is 38% of installed units; built-in suppression is estimated at $42 per unit. We do not have a substantiated suppression implementation timeline to share yet.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: The current customer-access clause risks disclosing identifiable company-specific per-model failure rates, which we cannot accept. We propose confidential detailed reporting to regulators and safety-relevant customer notices instead. Given the disclosed Hearth 10 result of 6.2%, an automatic sales bar at 5% would be disproportionate; a corrective-action plan and regulator review above 5% preserves oversight without an automatic market prohibition.

Ember 8’s 55°C sustained-heat failure rate was 3.9%, and its thermal-incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 units. Remote shut-off coverage is 81%; built-in suppression is estimated at $67 per unit. We do not have a substantiated suppression implementation timeline to share.

judge_section_notes: S1 is strong and applies to all thermal incidents, which constrains both companies' unreported incidents. S2 keeps the 5% failure rate as a corrective-action and regulator-review trigger with no sales stop, so Hearth 10 can stay on the market, while customers receive per-model numeric results. S5 keeps the 8/100k per-model trigger but makes recall discretionary with no mandatory recall, so Ember 8 is not automatically recalled.
